questions.question: What does `self` refer to inside an instance method?
options: The parent class only.
The Python interpreter.
A global variable.
The current instance.
questions.explanation: self is the specific object on which the method was called; it gives the method access to that object's attributes and other methods, not to the class definition or any global state.

questions.question: What does `__init__` typically do?
options: Initialize instance attributes for a newly created object.
Destroy objects that are no longer used.
Define all class methods automatically.
Make methods static by default.
questions.explanation: __init__ runs immediately after an object is created and sets up its initial attribute values; it does not destroy objects (that is __del__), define methods, or make anything static.

questions.question: What is the difference between class variables and instance variables?
options: They are exactly the same in behavior.
Instance variables are shared; class variables are private.
Class variables are shared; instance variables belong to each object.
Class variables only work in dataclasses.
questions.explanation: A class variable lives on the class itself and is shared by every instance; an instance variable is stored per object and isolated — mixing them up causes one object's changes to silently affect others.

questions.question: When should you usually prefer composition?
options: Only for global state containers.
When you can combine smaller objects instead of forcing inheritance hierarchy.
Never; inheritance is always cleaner.
Only when classes have no methods.
questions.explanation: Composition builds a class by holding instances of other classes rather than inheriting from them; it is more flexible because you can swap components at runtime without changing the class hierarchy.

questions.question: What problem appears if you accidentally use a class variable for per-user state?
options: One instance change can affect all instances unexpectedly.
Python refuses to run the class.
Methods become static automatically.
The variable becomes immutable.
questions.explanation: A class variable is shared across all instances; if one object mutates it, every other object sees the change immediately, which is almost never the intended behavior for per-user or per-request state.

questions.question: What is a good use case for a dataclass?
options: Any class that must use inheritance.
Replacing every function with a class.
A structured data model with many fields and simple behavior.
Code that never stores state.
questions.explanation: Dataclasses auto-generate __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from field declarations, eliminating repetitive boilerplate; they are ideal for value-holder objects but not for complex behavior-heavy classes.

questions.question: What happens if you forget `self` in an instance method signature?
options: The method becomes a class method.
Method calls usually fail with argument mismatch errors.
Python adds it automatically in every case.
Nothing; it still works as intended.
questions.explanation: Python silently passes the instance as the first argument when you call an instance method; if self is missing from the signature, Python maps it to the first declared parameter, causing a wrong-argument-count error.

questions.question: What is the strongest sign that a class is poorly designed?
options: It contains private helper methods.
It has an __init__ method.
It uses type hints.
It handles many unrelated responsibilities.
questions.explanation: A class that does too many unrelated things is hard to name accurately, hard to test in isolation, and hard to change without breaking unrelated behavior — the single-responsibility principle directly addresses this.
